segments.text: Negotiable instruments are written commercial instruments designed to facilitate payment and credit through transferable rights.

Prepare the three main instruments and parties to each, endorsement/negotiation, holder in due course, presentment, dishonour, discharge and special cheque rules. The subject is easiest through diagrams showing drawer, drawee, payee, maker and holder.
Primary authority: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, current official text.

A promissory note contains an unconditional undertaking by the maker to pay; a bill of exchange contains an unconditional order by the drawer directing the drawee to pay; a cheque is a bill drawn on a banker and payable according to the statutory definition. The official text of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 continues to define these instruments and related parties.
Learn the actors visually: maker/payee for a note; drawer/drawee/acceptor/payee for a bill; drawer/bank/payee for a cheque.

blocks.text: Negotiation and holder in due course

segments.text: Negotiation transfers an instrument in the legally recognized manner so that the transferee becomes holder. Endorsement and delivery are therefore not mere physical acts; their legal effect depends on the type of instrument and form of endorsement.
A holder in due course receives special protection when statutory conditions are satisfied. Do not assume every possessor or every transferee has that status.

Commercial certainty requires timely presentment and formal consequences when payment or acceptance is refused. Noting and protest record dishonour in the circumstances recognized by the Act, while notice of dishonour can preserve recourse against relevant parties.

Discharge may occur through payment or other legally recognized events. Exam questions should trace the instrument through creation → negotiation → presentment → honour/dishonour → recourse/discharge.

items.text: Learn the three main instruments through their parties and wording. A promissory note contains an undertaking to pay; a bill of exchange and cheque contain an order to pay, with a cheque drawn on a banker.

Negotiability allows rights embodied in the instrument to be transferred by the legally prescribed method. Endorsement and delivery rules matter because physical possession alone may not always be enough.
A holder in due course receives special statutory protection if the legal requirements are satisfied. This concept should be compared with an ordinary holder.
Presentment, dishonour, notice, noting and protest are sequential commercial-law concepts. Discharge concerns the ending of liability on the instrument in recognized circumstances.
Draw diagrams showing maker, drawer, drawee, payee, endorser and holder. Visualizing the parties prevents most conceptual confusion.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not say a cheque is the same as a promissory note. One contains an order on a bank; the other contains a promise by the maker.

items.text: Draw party diagrams for cheque, bill and promissory note.
Prepare holder vs holder in due course.
Study dishonour and discharge as separate stages.
